final_answer:
For any nonzero solution \(x(t)\), write \(r(t)=\|x(t)\|_2\) and \(u(t)=x(t)/\|x(t)\|_2\). Then, whenever \(\sigma(t)=i\),

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\log r(t)
= u(t)^T \frac{A_i+A_i^T}{2}u(t).
\]

But

\[
\frac{A_1+A_1^T}{2}
=
\frac{A_2+A_2^T}{2}
=
S
=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\alpha & \kappa/2\\
\kappa/2 & -\beta
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore the instantaneous Euclidean norm growth rate is independent of the chosen switch, and is always at most the largest eigenvalue of \(S\). Hence for every switching signal,

\[
\|\Phi_\sigma(t)\|_2\le e^{\lambda_{\max}(S)t},
\]

so

\[
\Lambda(\alpha,\beta,\kappa)\le \lambda_{\max}(S).
\]

The eigenvalues of \(S\) are

\[
-\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}
\pm
\frac12\sqrt{(\alpha-\beta)^2+\kappa^2}.
\]

Thus

\[
\lambda_{\max}(S)
=
-\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}
+
\frac12\sqrt{(\alpha-\beta)^2+\kappa^2}.
\]

It remains to see this upper bound is sharp. Switch periodically, spending time \(h\) in mode \(1\), then time \(h\) in mode \(2\). The monodromy over one period is

\[
M_h=e^{A_2h}e^{A_1h}.
\]

As \(h\to0\),

\[
e^{A_2h}e^{A_1h}
=
\exp\bigl((A_1+A_2)h+O(h^2)\bigr)
=
\exp\bigl(2Sh+O(h^2)\bigr).
\]

Therefore the exponential growth rate of this periodic switching tends to

\[
\lambda_{\max}(S).
\]

Since the definition takes a supremum over all admissible switchings, the upper bound is attained in the supremal sense.

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\Lambda(\alpha,\beta,\kappa)
=
-\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}
+
\frac12\sqrt{(\alpha-\beta)^2+\kappa^2}
}.
\]
